09.01.title: Atomic bonding and stiffness
09.01.html:
Why is steel about 200 times stiffer than rubber and 3 times stiffer than aluminium? Young’s modulus is not a property you can change by heat treatment or cold work, unlike strength. It’s set by the bonds between atoms: how steeply the energy rises when you pull two atoms apart.

The pair potential

Two atoms attract at long range and repel strongly when their electron clouds overlap. A classic model is the Lennard-Jones potential:

V(r)=4ε[(rσ​)12−(rσ​)6].

It has a minimum of depth ε at r0​=21/6σ, the equilibrium spacing. The force between the atoms is F=−dV/dr, which is zero at r0​.

Stiffness is curvature

Expand V around r0​:

V(r)≈−ε+21​S(r−r0​)2,S=dr2d2V​​r0​​.

So for small stretches each bond is a linear spring of stiffness S: Hooke’s law, straight from the shape of the energy well. For Lennard-Jones, S=72ε/(21/3σ2)=57.1ε/σ2.

From bonds to Young’s modulus

In a simple cubic packing, each bond carries the load on an area of about r02​, and a strain ϵ stretches it by ϵr0​. Stress =Sϵr0​/r02​, so

E≈r0​S​.

Covalent and metallic bonds have S of about 20 to 200 N/m at r0​≈0.25 nm, giving E of 80 to 800 GPa: metals and ceramics. Weak van der Waals bonds, as in solid argon or between polymer chains, have S≈1 N/m and give E of a few GPa. Rubber is softer still because it doesn’t stretch bonds at all, it uncoils chains.

Two bonus results

  • The attraction is largest at 1.109r0​. That maximum force sets a theoretical strength of roughly E/10 to E/30. Real materials fail far below it, for reasons covered in 09.03 and 09.12.
  • The well is steeper on the inside than the outside. A vibrating (hot) pair spends its time further apart on average: thermal expansion.

Worked exampleArgon, from potential to modulus

ε=1.65×10−21 J (10.3 meV), σ=0.340 nm.

  1. r0​=21/6⋅0.340=0.3816 nm.
  2. Bond stiffness: the analytic formula gives 0.8157 N/m, and a central finite difference of V gives 0.8157 N/m. The slope of the force at r0​ is −S, as it should be.
  3. E≈S/r0​=2.14 GPa. Measured values for solid argon are about 1 to 3 GPa.
  4. Peak attraction 11.63 pN at 1.1087r0​ (strain 0.109). Stress estimate 80 MPa, which is E/26.8.
  5. Vibrating with 5 % of the well depth, the turning points are 0.9669 and 1.0431 r0​, so the midpoint moves out to 1.0050 r0​. At 20 %, 1.0220 r0​. That growth is thermal expansion.
  6. A metal-like bond with S=50 N/m at 0.25 nm gives E≈200 GPa, about right for steel.

Exercise 1A stiffer bond

A diamond C–C bond has a stiffness of about 470 N/m at r0​=0.154 nm. Estimate Young’s modulus with E≈S/r0​ and compare it with the measured 1050 to 1200 GPa.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. E≈470/0.154×10−9=3.05×1012 Pa, about 3000 GPa.
  2. That is about 2.7 times the measured value. The simple-cubic picture assumes every bond lines up with the load. In diamond’s tetrahedral network the bonds are tilted, so they also bend and rotate, and fewer bonds cross each square metre. The estimate gets the order of magnitude right, which is what it is for.

09.02.title: Crystal structures
09.02.html:
A Swiss watch spring, an aluminium bike frame and a copper wire are all crystals: their atoms sit on a regular three-dimensional grid. Which grid a metal chooses decides a lot. Copper and aluminium (face-centred cubic) are ductile even at low temperature, iron at room temperature (body-centred cubic) can turn brittle in the cold, and titanium and magnesium (hexagonal) are harder to form.

Unit cells

A crystal is a small unit cell repeated in all directions. For metals, model the atoms as hard spheres of radius R that touch their nearest neighbours. Three cubic cells, with lattice constant a:

lattice atoms per cell atoms touch along R coordination
simple cubic (SC) 1 edge a/2 6
body-centred cubic (BCC) 2 body diagonal 3​a/4 8
face-centred cubic (FCC) 4 face diagonal 2​a/4 12

Atoms on corners are shared by 8 cells, those on faces by 2. So FCC has 8⋅81​+6⋅21​=4 atoms per cell.

Packing factor

The atomic packing factor is the fraction of space filled by atoms:

APF=a3n⋅34​πR3​.

For FCC, 4⋅34​π(2​a/4)3/a3=π/18​=0.7405, the densest possible packing of equal spheres. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) stacks the same close-packed layers in a different order and reaches the same 0.7405. BCC gives 0.680, SC only 0.524 (polonium is the only element that uses it).

Density from the lattice

ρ=NA​a3nA​,

with A the molar mass. X-ray diffraction measures a very precisely, so this links atomic structure to bulk density.

Worked exampleBuilding lattices in code

  1. The code generates lattice points, counts neighbours at the smallest distance, and computes the packing factor from the formula and by Monte Carlo (400,000 random points in the cell):
lattice coordination APF formula APF Monte Carlo
SC 6 0.5236 0.5235
BCC 8 0.6802 0.6803
FCC 12 0.7405 0.7403
  1. HCP with the ideal c/a=1.6330: coordination 12 and APF 0.7405, equal to π/18​.
  2. Densities: iron (BCC, a=0.28665 nm) 7.874 g/cm³; copper (FCC, 0.36149 nm) 8.935 g/cm³; aluminium (FCC, 0.40495 nm) 2.699 g/cm³. All match handbook values.

Exercise 1Nickel

Nickel is FCC with an atomic radius of 0.1246 nm and a molar mass of 58.69 g/mol. Find the lattice constant and the density.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4R=2​a, so a=4⋅0.1246/2​=0.3524 nm.
  2. ρ=4⋅58.69/(6.022×1023⋅(0.3524×10−7 cm)3)=8.91 g/cm³ (handbook value 8.90).

09.03.title: Defects and dislocations
09.03.html:
In the 1920s physicists calculated how strong a perfect metal crystal should be in shear. The answer was thousands of times stronger than any real metal. Either the theory was wrong, or real crystals had a defect that let them slip easily. In 1934 Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi independently proposed it: the dislocation. Seen directly in electron microscopes in the 1950s, dislocations explain why metals yield, why they work-harden, and why they can be bent instead of shattering.

The ideal shear strength

Slide one plane of atoms over another by x. The resisting stress must repeat every atomic spacing b. Frenkel modelled it as a sine:

τ(x)=τmax​sinb2πx​.

For small x this must reduce to Hooke’s law, τ=Gx/a with a the spacing between planes. Matching slopes gives

τmax​=2πaGb​≈2πG​.

For copper, G=48 GPa gives about 7.6 GPa. A pure copper single crystal actually starts slipping at around 0.5 MPa, some 15,000 times less.

Dislocations

Instead of a whole plane slipping at once, imagine an extra half-plane of atoms squeezed into the crystal: an edge dislocation. Under shear only the bonds near its core need to break and re-form, one row at a time, like moving a ruck along a carpet instead of dragging the whole carpet. The stress needed (the Peierls stress) is tiny for metals with wide, smeared-out dislocation cores. When it has crossed the crystal, the top has moved by one spacing b, the Burgers vector.

Most metallurgy is the art of making dislocations harder to move: grain boundaries, dissolved atoms, fine precipitates and tangles of other dislocations all get in their way (09.05).

A one-dimensional model

The Frenkel-Kontorova chain captures the idea. A row of atoms joined by springs k rests on a wavy substrate with wells one spacing apart. Push every atom with force F:

  • A perfect row slips only when F exceeds the substrate’s maximum restoring force.
  • Put one extra atom in (a kink, the 1D analogue of a dislocation). It glides at a far smaller push, because the atoms near it sit partway up the wells already.

Worked exampleIdeal strength and a gliding kink

  1. Copper: G/(2π)=7.64 GPa. Measured single-crystal yield is about 0.5 MPa, a ratio of 15,279.
  2. The chain: 60 sites, spring k=4, substrate amplitude V0​=0.2 (units where a=1). A perfect chain slips at F=V0​π=0.6283 per atom, verified: it holds at 95 % of that and slips at 105 %.
  3. With one extra atom, relaxed to a kink centred at site 29.5 (tightest spacing 0.715), bisection on F finds that the kink starts to glide at F=0.00766, 82 times less than rigid slip.
  4. Softer springs make a narrower kink that is harder to move: k=2 needs 0.06016 (10.4 times less than rigid slip) and k=1 needs 0.18940 (3.3 times less). Wide dislocation cores, as in FCC metals, are why those metals are so easy to deform.

Exercise 1Aluminium and iron

Estimate the ideal shear strength of aluminium (G=26 GPa) and iron (G=82 GPa). Annealed pure aluminium yields in tension at about 30 MPa, and soft iron at about 150 MPa. Taking the shear yield as half the tensile yield, how many times below ideal are they?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Aluminium: 26/2π=4.14 GPa. Shear yield about 15 MPa, so 4140/15=276 times below ideal.
  2. Iron: 82/2π=13.05 GPa. Shear yield about 75 MPa, so 174 times below.
  3. Both are polycrystals with some impurities, so they’re far stronger than a pure single crystal, but still two orders of magnitude below ideal. Only tiny defect-free whiskers and nanopillars come close to G/2π.

09.04.title: The tensile test
09.04.html:
Almost every strength number you’ll use, from yield strength in a datasheet to the allowable stress in a code, starts with one test: pull a standard bar until it breaks and record the load and the stretch. Reading that curve properly is a core skill.

Engineering and true stress

A round bar of original area A0​ and gauge length L0​ carries load P and stretches by ΔL.

  • Engineering stress and strain use the original dimensions: s=P/A0​ and e=ΔL/L0​.
  • True stress and strain use the current ones: σ=P/A and ε=ln(L/L0​).

Plastic deformation keeps the volume constant, AL=A0​L0​, so before necking

σ=s(1+e),ε=ln(1+e).

Reading the curve

  1. Young’s modulus E: the slope of the straight initial part. Fit a line well inside the elastic region, and use its zero crossing to correct for slack in the grips.
  2. 0.2 % offset yield Rp0.2​: most metals have no sharp yield point. Draw a line of slope E starting at 0.2 % strain; where it cuts the curve is the yield strength.
  3. Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the maximum engineering stress.
  4. Elongation: the strain at fracture (ductility).

Necking: the Considère criterion

The load is P=σA. As the bar stretches, σ rises (work hardening) but A falls. The load peaks when dP=0:

dεdσ​=σ.

Past that point any thinner spot carries more stress than its hardening can resist, and a neck forms. For a material with σ=Kεn (Hollomon), necking starts at a true strain of exactly ε=n, with

UTS=Knne−n.

So the hardening exponent n tells you how far a sheet can stretch evenly, which matters for forming car panels (09.22).

Worked exampleProcessing a raw test

A round aluminium-alloy bar, d0​=6 mm (A0​=28.274 mm²), extensometer gauge 30 mm. The data are synthetic so the answer is known: E=69 GPa, σ=380εp0.06​ MPa, with 5 N of load-cell noise and 0.5 µm of extensometer noise, 4000 points up to necking.

  1. Linear fit between 10 % and 40 % of the maximum load: E=68.69 GPa.
  2. 0.2 % offset line, with linear interpolation at the crossing: yield 259.90 MPa. The exact value is 380⋅0.0020.06=261.73 MPa, so the error is 0.7 %, inside the 1 % target.
  3. UTS 301.16 MPa against Considère’s Knne−n=302.28 MPa. Uniform elongation 6.55 % against 6.68 % predicted (the top of the curve is very flat, so noise blurs where the maximum is).
  4. At necking the true stress, 320.98 MPa, equals the hardening slope nKεn−1 = 320.98 MPa.

Exercise 1A steel test

A steel bar of 10 mm diameter yields (0.2 % offset) at a load of 27.5 kN and reaches a maximum of 36.1 kN at an extension of 9.0 mm over a 50 mm gauge. Find the yield strength, the UTS, and the true stress and true strain at the UTS.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A0​=π⋅102/4=78.54 mm². Yield =27500/78.54=350.1 MPa.
  2. UTS =36100/78.54=459.6 MPa.
  3. e=9/50=0.18. True stress =459.6⋅1.18=542.3 MPa; true strain =ln1.18=0.1655.
  4. By Considère that true strain is about the hardening exponent: n≈0.17, typical for mild steel.

09.05.title: Hardening mechanisms
09.05.html:
Pure annealed iron yields at about 100 MPa. The steel in a Swiss watch spring yields at over 1500 MPa. It’s mostly the same iron atoms, with the same Young’s modulus. The difference is how hard it is for dislocations to move. Every strengthening method puts obstacles in their way.

Four ways to block dislocations

  1. Grain boundaries. A dislocation can’t easily cross from one crystal orientation to the next, so dislocations pile up at boundaries. Smaller grains mean shorter pile-ups and more boundaries. This gives the Hall-Petch relation
σy​=σ0​+d​k​,

with d the grain size, σ0​ the friction stress of the lattice, and k a material constant (about 0.74 MPa√m for mild steel, 0.07 for aluminium). It’s the only mechanism that raises strength without losing toughness.

  1. Solid solution. Dissolved atoms of a different size strain the lattice around them and pin dislocations. Brass (copper with zinc) and Al-Mg alloys use it. The effect grows roughly with the square root of concentration.

  2. Precipitation. Fine particles of a second phase. A dislocation either cuts through them or bows out between them and leaves a loop behind (Orowan). Bowing between particles spaced L apart needs a shear stress of

τ≈LGb​,

so closer particles mean higher strength. Age-hardened aluminium bike frames (6061-T6, 7075-T6) get most of their strength this way.

  1. Work hardening. Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and block each other. Cold-rolled sheet and drawn wire are strengthened this way; annealing undoes it.

To convert a shear stress on the slip plane to a tensile yield stress for a polycrystal, multiply by the Taylor factor, about 3.06 for FCC metals.

Worked exampleFitting Hall-Petch data

Synthetic data for a mild steel with σ0​=70 MPa and k=0.74 MPa√m, at eight grain sizes from 5 to 200 µm, with 4 MPa of scatter.

  1. Measured yields: 400.9 MPa at 5 µm, down to 127.7 MPa at 200 µm.
  2. Least squares on σy​ against d−1/2: σ0​=70.08±2.32 MPa and k=0.7376±0.0091 MPa√m. The fitted slope recovers 0.74 within 0.3 %, well inside its standard error.
  3. Predictions: 174 MPa at 50 µm, 303 MPa at 10 µm, 808 MPa at 1 µm. Ultra-fine-grained steels are made by controlled rolling.
  4. Orowan in aluminium (G=26 GPa, b=0.286 nm, Taylor factor 3.06): precipitates 1000 nm apart add 23 MPa; 100 nm apart, 228 MPa; 30 nm apart, 758 MPa.

Exercise 1Grain refinement

An aluminium alloy has σ0​=25 MPa and k=0.068 MPa√m. By how much does refining the grains from 100 µm to 10 µm raise the yield strength?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At 100 µm: 25+0.068/10−4​=25+6.8=31.8 MPa.
  2. At 10 µm: 25+0.068/10−5​=25+21.5=46.5 MPa.
  3. The increase is 14.7 MPa, much less than in steel, because aluminium’s k is ten times smaller. Aluminium alloys rely mainly on precipitation instead.

09.06.title: Phase diagrams
09.06.html:
Melt copper and nickel together and let the mixture cool. Unlike a pure metal, it doesn’t freeze at one temperature. Over a range of about 25 °C, solid crystals richer in nickel grow inside a liquid richer in copper. Phase diagrams are the maps that tell you, for any composition and temperature, which phases are present, what they’re made of and how much of each there is.

Reading a binary diagram

The horizontal axis is composition (here, % nickel), the vertical one temperature. Copper and nickel dissolve in each other completely in both liquid and solid, so their diagram is a simple lens between two curves:

  • above the liquidus, all liquid;
  • below the solidus, all solid;
  • between them, liquid and solid coexist.

Inside the two-phase region, draw a horizontal tie line through your point. Its ends, on the liquidus and solidus, give the compositions xL​ and xS​ of the liquid and the solid.

The lever rule

How much of each phase? Conservation of nickel: if a fraction fL​ is liquid and fS​=1−fL​ is solid, then fL​xL​+fS​xS​=x0​. Solving,

fL​=xS​−xL​xS​−x0​​,fS​=xS​−xL​x0​−xL​​.

It’s like a lever balanced at x0​: each phase’s fraction is the length of the arm on the opposite side, divided by the whole tie line.

Where the curves come from

For an ideal solution, each component’s equilibrium between liquid and solid depends only on its own melting point Tm​ and heat of fusion ΔH:

xS​xL​​=exp[RΔH​(Tm​1​−T1​)].

Writing that for both copper and nickel gives two equations for xL​ and xS​ at each temperature, so the whole lens follows from four handbook numbers. Real alloys deviate somewhat, and many systems have eutectics, intermediate compounds and solid-state changes (09.07), but the tie-line and lever-rule reasoning is the same everywhere.

Worked exampleA 40 % nickel alloy

Copper: Tm​=1358 K, ΔH=13.05 kJ/mol. Nickel: 1728 K, 17.48 kJ/mol.

  1. Phase boundaries from the ideal-solution model (% Ni in liquid / solid): 1100 °C, 3.3 / 4.5; 1200 °C, 26.9 / 33.3; 1300 °C, 53.5 / 60.3; 1400 °C, 82.8 / 86.2.
  2. At 1235 °C: liquid with 35.9 % Ni and solid with 42.9 % Ni. Lever rule: 41.2 % liquid and 58.8 % solid. The two fractions sum to 1 exactly, and they reproduce the overall 40 % Ni to 10−12.
  3. Bisection on each boundary: the alloy starts to freeze at 1250.6 °C and is fully solid at 1224.5 °C.
  4. Cooled fast, the first solid (richer in Ni) has no time to even out, giving composition gradients called coring. A homogenising anneal fixes it.

Exercise 1Reading a tie line

On a measured Cu-Ni diagram at 1250 °C, the liquidus is at 32 wt% Ni and the solidus at 43 wt% Ni. An alloy has 35 wt% Ni. What fractions (by mass) are liquid and solid?

Show step-by-step solution

  2. fS​=(35−32)/11=0.273.
  3. Check: 0.727⋅32+0.273⋅43=35.0 wt% Ni.

09.07.title: Steel and heat treatment
09.07.html:
A blacksmith heats a knife blade until it glows cherry red, plunges it into water, then reheats it gently until it turns straw coloured. Each step changes the arrangement of carbon atoms inside the iron. Steel is iron with less than about 2 % carbon, and that small amount of carbon, together with the heat treatment, is what lets one alloy family cover everything from soft car body panels to razor blades.

The steel corner of the Fe-C diagram

Iron changes crystal structure with temperature. Below 912 °C pure iron is BCC ferrite (α), which dissolves almost no carbon (0.022 % at most). Above that it’s FCC austenite (γ), whose larger holes hold up to 2.11 % carbon. Carbon that doesn’t fit forms the hard compound cementite, Fe₃C, with 6.70 % C.

The key point is the eutectoid: at 727 °C and 0.76 % C, austenite turns into ferrite and cementite at the same time, in thin alternating plates called pearlite.

  • Hypoeutectoid steel (less than 0.76 % C): on slow cooling, ferrite grows first along the austenite grain boundaries. The rest of the austenite turns into pearlite at 727 °C.
  • Hypereutectoid steel (more than 0.76 % C): cementite forms first, then pearlite.

The lever rule (09.06), applied just above 727 °C, gives the fraction of proeutectoid ferrite for a hypoeutectoid steel with carbon content c:

fα​=0.76−0.0220.76−c​,fpearlite​=1−fα​.

Quenching and tempering

Cool austenite fast enough and the carbon has no time to diffuse out and form pearlite. The FCC lattice shears into a strained, body-centred tetragonal structure called martensite, which is very hard and brittle. Tempering (reheating to 200 to 600 °C) lets a little carbon precipitate as fine carbides. It trades some hardness for a lot of toughness.

Whether a bar becomes martensite depends on how fast it cools between 800 and 500 °C. For a small bar, lumped cooling (as in Phase 07) gives

t8/5​=4hρcp​D​ln500−Tf​800−Tf​​,

with D the diameter, h the film coefficient of the quench fluid and Tf​ the fluid temperature. Plain carbon steels need a t8/5​ of about a second, so only water works, and only on thin sections. Alloying with chromium, molybdenum or nickel slows the pearlite reaction, so oil or even air can harden thicker parts. That property is called hardenability.

Worked exampleMicrostructure and quench times

  1. With 0.45 % C (a typical shaft steel), proeutectoid ferrite is (0.76−0.45)/(0.76−0.022)=42.0 % and pearlite 58.0 %. Overall cementite: (0.45−0.022)/(6.70−0.022)=6.41 %.
  2. Pearlite itself is (0.76−0.022)/(6.70−0.022)=11.1 % cementite plates.
  3. Carbon balance, fα​⋅0.022+fFe₃C​⋅6.70, gives back the alloy’s carbon content to 10−12 for every composition tested.
  4. A 25 mm bar (ρ=7850 kg/m³, cp​=600 J/(kg K)) cooling into fluid at 20 °C: 286 s in still air (h=50), 9.5 s in oil (h=1500), 2.9 s in water (h=5000).
  5. The Biot number in water is hD/(4k)=0.78, well above 0.1. The core cools much more slowly than the surface, so even water-quenched plain carbon bars may harden only in a surface shell.

Exercise 1A 0.2 % carbon steel

After slow cooling, what fractions of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite does a 0.20 % C steel have? Roughly estimate its hardness, taking ferrite as 80 HB and pearlite as 250 HB.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. fα​=(0.76−0.20)/(0.76−0.022)=0.56/0.738=0.759.
  2. Pearlite: 0.241.
  3. Hardness: 0.759⋅80+0.241⋅250=60.7+60.2=121 HB. That’s soft and easy to weld, typical of structural steel.

09.08.title: Diffusion
09.08.html:
A gear has to be hard on the surface to resist wear, but tough in the core so its teeth don’t snap. One way to get both is to pack a low-carbon steel gear in a carbon-rich atmosphere at about 900 °C for a few hours. Carbon atoms wander in from the surface, giving a hard case once the gear is quenched. How deep they get is a diffusion problem.

Fick’s laws

Atoms jump randomly between lattice sites. Where there are more atoms on one side than the other, more jump down the gradient than up. Fick’s first law gives the flux:

J=−D∂x∂C​.

Conservation of atoms then gives Fick’s second law, which is the same equation as heat conduction (Phase 07):

∂t∂C​=D∂x2∂2C​.

Diffusivity and temperature

Each jump needs an activation energy Q, so D follows an Arrhenius law:

D=D0​e−Q/RT.

For carbon in austenite, D0​=2.3×10−5 m²/s and Q=148 kJ/mol. A 100 °C rise roughly triples D.

The carburising solution

A thick part, initially at carbon content C0​, whose surface is held at Cs​ from time zero, has the profile

C(x,t)=Cs​−(Cs​−C0​)erf(2Dt​x​).

The error function rises from 0 to almost 1 as its argument goes from 0 to 2. Any particular concentration sits at a fixed value of x/Dt​, so

x∝Dt​.

Doubling the case depth takes four times as long. The quantity Dt​ is the diffusion length. It’s the quick estimate for how far atoms get in a given time, in welding, semiconductor doping and corrosion alike.

Worked exampleCarburising a gear

Surface 1.0 % C, steel 0.2 % C, case defined at 0.4 % C.

  1. At 927 °C (1200.15 K): D=2.3×10−5e−148000/(8.314⋅1200.15)=8.32×10−12 m²/s.
  2. We need erf(z)=(1.0−0.4)/(1.0−0.2)=0.75, so z=0.8134.
  3. After 4 h: x=2⋅0.81348.32×10−12⋅14400​=0.563 mm.
  4. At 1027 °C, D=2.60×10−11 m²/s, and the same depth takes only 1.28 h.
  5. An explicit finite-difference solution of Fick’s second law matches the erf profile to 3.4×10−5 % C everywhere.

Exercise 1A deeper case

How long at 927 °C does the gear need for a case depth of 1.0 mm?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Depth goes as t​, so t=4 h×(1.0/0.563)2.
  2. (1.0/0.563)2=3.155, giving 12.6 h.
  3. That’s why deep cases are expensive, and why carburising is pushed to higher temperatures when the furnace and grain growth allow.

09.09.title: Polymers and viscoelasticity
09.09.html:
Tighten a plastic hose clamp and come back a month later: it’s loose. Hang a weight from a nylon line and it slowly stretches. Metals at room temperature behave elastically: release the load and they spring back, regardless of how long it was applied. Polymers are long tangled chains that slide past each other given time, so their response depends on time and temperature. They’re partly solid, partly liquid: viscoelastic.

Chains and temperature

A polymer is thousands of repeating units joined into a chain. Polyethylene is just −CH2​− repeated. Below its glass transition temperature Tg​, an amorphous polymer is glassy and stiff (acrylic, polystyrene at room temperature). Above Tg​ the chains can wriggle and it becomes rubbery (rubber, polyethylene). Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded. Thermosets (epoxy) and elastomers have chemical cross-links between chains and don’t melt.

Springs and dashpots

Model the elastic part as a spring, σ=Eε, and the viscous part as a dashpot, σ=ηε˙. The ratio τ=η/E is a time constant.

  • Maxwell model (spring and dashpot in series). Hold the strain fixed and the stress relaxes:
σ(t)=Eε0​e−t/τ.
  • Kelvin-Voigt model (spring and dashpot in parallel). Apply a constant stress and the strain creeps towards σ/E:
ε(t)=Eσ​(1−e−t/τ).

Neither model alone looks like a real polymer: Maxwell flows forever under load, and Kelvin-Voigt has no instant stretch. The standard linear solid (a spring E1​ in series with a Kelvin-Voigt unit E2​, η) gives an instant strain σ/E1​ followed by delayed creep up to σ/E1​+σ/E2​.

Design consequence: for a plastic part under sustained load, use the creep modulus at the design life and temperature, which can be half the short-term modulus or less.

Worked exampleRelaxation and creep

Polymer with E=2 GPa and η=2×1012 Pa s, so τ=1000 s.

  1. Held at 1 % strain (initial stress 20 MPa), a fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration gives 7.36 MPa after 1000 s and 1.00 MPa after 3000 s. The exact values are 20e−1=7.36 and 20e−3=0.996, matched to 0.1 %.
  2. Kelvin-Voigt under 10 MPa: strain 0.3161 % after one τ, exactly 0.5(1−e−1) %.
  3. A nylon-like standard linear solid (E1​=3 GPa, E2​=6 GPa, retardation time 1 h) under 15 MPa: 0.500 % instantly, 0.658 % after 1 h, 0.738 % after 3 h and 0.750 % after 10 h. The long-term effective modulus is 2 GPa, a third below the instant 3 GPa.

Exercise 1A snap-fit losing its grip

A polypropylene snap fit is bent to a fixed strain, producing 12 MPa. Its relaxation time is about 2 days (Maxwell model). What is the holding stress after a week?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. t/τ=7/2=3.5.
  2. σ=12e−3.5=12⋅0.0302=0.36 MPa.
  3. Almost nothing is left. That’s why snap fits are designed to be stress-free once engaged, and why plastic parts under constant load use creep data rather than the datasheet modulus.

09.10.title: Composites
09.10.html:
A carbon-fibre bike frame weighs under a kilogram and is stiffer than steel, but drop it on a sharp edge and it can crack where the fibres weren’t pointing. A composite is two materials combined: strong, stiff fibres (carbon, glass, aramid, flax) held in place by a softer matrix (epoxy, polyester). The fibres carry the load; the matrix transfers it between fibres and protects them. The catch is that the result is only stiff in the directions the fibres point.

Rule of mixtures

With fibre volume fraction Vf​, loading along the fibres strains both constituents equally (springs in parallel):

E1​=Vf​Ef​+(1−Vf​)Em​(Voigt).

Loading across the fibres puts them in series, so the stresses are equal and the soft matrix dominates:

E2​1​=Ef​Vf​​+Em​1−Vf​​(Reuss).

These two are upper and lower bounds on the stiffness of any mixture with these volume fractions.

Off-axis loading

Load a unidirectional ply at angle θ to its fibres and the modulus falls off fast:

Ex​1​=E1​cos4θ​+(G12​1​−E1​2ν12​​)sin2θcos2θ+E2​sin4θ​.

Laminates

Real parts stack plies at different angles. Classical lamination theory rotates each ply’s stiffness matrix to the laminate axes and adds them, weighted by thickness. A symmetric stack such as [0/+45/−45/90]s​ is quasi-isotropic: the same in-plane stiffness in every direction, at roughly a third of the unidirectional value. Designers choose layups so fibres follow the loads, for example ±45° plies in a tube to carry torsion.

Worked exampleA carbon/epoxy ply and laminate

Fibre: Ef​=230 GPa, Gf​=15 GPa, νf​=0.2. Epoxy: Em​=3.5 GPa, Gm​=1.3 GPa, νm​=0.35. Vf​=0.6.

  1. E1​=0.6⋅230+0.4⋅3.5=139.4 GPa. E2​=1/(0.6/230+0.4/3.5)=8.55 GPa. G12​=2.88 GPa (Reuss), ν12​=0.26.
  2. Off-axis: 103.5 GPa at 5°, 35.4 at 15°, 13.2 at 30°, 8.5 at 45°. Just 15° of misalignment costs three quarters of the stiffness.
  3. Rotating the stiffness matrix numerically gives the same Ex​ as the closed form to 10−6.
  4. Quasi-isotropic [0/45/−45/90]s​: 51.58 GPa at 0°, 22.5°, 45° and 70°, identical to 10−6.
  5. With density 0.6⋅1800+0.4⋅1200=1560 kg/m³, its specific stiffness is 33.1 MJ/kg against 25.9 for aluminium. Even the quasi-isotropic layup wins, and tailored layups win by far more.

Exercise 1Glass fibre

E-glass fibres (Ef​=72 GPa) in polyester (Em​=3 GPa) at Vf​=0.5. Find E1​ and E2​.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. E1​=0.5⋅72+0.5⋅3=37.5 GPa.
  2. E2​=1/(0.5/72+0.5/3)=1/(0.006944+0.16667)=5.76 GPa.
  3. The ratio is 6.5, smaller than for carbon (16), because glass fibres are less stiff relative to the matrix.

09.11.title: Bamboo and wood
09.11.html:
In Bali you can see three-storey buildings framed entirely in bamboo. A culm (the stem) grows to full height in a few months, needs no processing beyond drying and treatment, and can rival steel in strength per kilogram. Bamboo and wood are natural fibre composites (09.10), and nature has optimised their structure for bending loads: wind on a tall stem.

Fibres along the stem

Wood is made of hollow cellulose cells aligned along the trunk, glued by lignin. Bamboo has bundles of stiff fibres (around 40 GPa) embedded in soft parenchyma tissue. Both are strongly anisotropic. Spruce has E≈12 GPa along the grain but under 1 GPa across it, so timber splits easily along the grain and must be loaded along it.

The hollow tube

For bending, what matters is the second moment of area I (Phase 05), and material far from the neutral axis counts most. Take a fixed amount of material (area A). A solid rod of diameter d has I=πd4/64. Spread the same area into a thin tube of outer diameter D and the ratio is

Isolid​Itube​​=d2D2+Di2​​,

which grows without limit as the tube gets wider. The limit is local buckling of a thin wall, which bamboo prevents with nodes: solid diaphragms every 20 to 40 cm.

Functional grading

Bamboo goes further: its fibre fraction rises from about 15 % at the inner wall to 60 % at the outer skin. With modulus E(r) varying through the wall,

EI=∫E(r)r2dA=∫ri​ro​​E(r)πr3dr,

so moving fibres outward raises the bending stiffness without adding any material.

Engineering with natural materials

Natural materials vary: density, moisture, knots, splits. Their design values come from statistics (09.30), and they need protection from insects, rot and UV. Bamboo is also hard to join, since you can’t weld it and bolts split it, so engineered joints often fill the end internodes with mortar.

Worked exampleA 100 mm culm

Culm with outer diameter 100 mm and wall 10 mm: A=2827 mm², I=2.898×106 mm⁴.

  1. A solid rod of the same area has d=60.0 mm and I=0.636×106 mm⁴. The culm is 4.56 times stiffer for the same mass. Check: (1002+802)/602=4.56.
  2. Fibre fraction rising linearly from 15 % inside to 60 % outside averages 38.3 % over the ring. Integrating E(r)πr3 gives EI=49.8 kN m².
  3. The same fibres spread evenly give 48.0 kN m², exactly EˉI. Grading adds 3.8 % for free.
  4. Total advantage over a uniform solid rod of the same mass: 4.56×1.038=4.7 times.

Exercise 1A wider culm

Keep the area at 2827 mm² but make the culm 140 mm across. What is the wall thickness and how much stiffer is it than the solid rod (ignore grading)?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Di2​=1402−4⋅2827/π=19600−3600=16000, so Di​=126.5 mm and the wall is 6.75 mm.
  2. Itube​/Isolid​=(19600+16000)/3600=9.89.
  3. Twice as stiff again as the 100 mm culm, but with a wall of only 6.8 mm it’s far more prone to local buckling and crushing at joints.

09.12.title: Fracture mechanics
09.12.html:
On 16 January 1943 the tanker SS Schenectady, moored in calm water, split in two with a bang heard a mile away. The welded steel was well below its yield stress. The cause was a small crack in a brittle weld on a cold night. Strength alone doesn’t tell you whether a part will break: you need to know how it tolerates cracks. That’s fracture mechanics.

Griffith’s energy balance

A crack of length 2a in a plate under stress σ releases stored elastic energy roughly from a region of size a around it, πσ2a2/E per unit thickness. Making the crack costs surface energy 4aγ (two faces, two tips). The total

U(a)=4aγ−Eπσ2a2​

rises, peaks, and falls. Beyond the peak, growing the crack releases more energy than it costs, so it runs. The peak is at

a∗=πσ22Eγ​.

Stress intensity

Near any crack tip the stresses go as 1/r​ with a strength set by one number, the stress intensity factor:

K=Yσπa​,

with Y a geometry factor (1 for a central crack in a wide plate, 1.12 for an edge crack). Fast fracture happens when K reaches the material’s fracture toughness KIC​. So the critical crack size is

ac​=π1​(YσKIC​​)2.

Some typical values of KIC​ in MPa√m: glass 0.75, aluminium 7075-T6 about 25, structural steel 50 or more (much less when cold), tough pressure-vessel steel 150.

Using it

  • Inspection: the smallest crack you can reliably find must be well below ac​.
  • Halving the stress quadruples the tolerable crack.
  • Leak before break: a pressure vessel should be tough enough that a crack grows right through the wall, and leaks visibly, while still subcritical.

Worked exampleGlass and steel

  1. Glass with E=70 GPa and γ=1 J/m² at 50 MPa: scanning U(a) numerically puts the peak at a half-length of 17.83 µm, matching 2Eγ/(πσ2). The equivalent KIC​=2Eγ​=0.374 MPa√m. Real glass is about twice that.
  2. Edge cracks at 300 MPa (Y=1.12): critical depth 7.05 mm in structural steel (KIC​=50), 63.4 mm in pressure-vessel steel (150) and 1.76 mm in 7075-T6 aluminium (25).
  3. A vessel with a 12 mm wall and KIC​=150: a through crack (a=6 mm) stays subcritical up to 150/π⋅0.006​=1093 MPa. That’s far above the 400 MPa yield, so it leaks before it breaks.

Exercise 1A cold weld

A steel’s toughness falls to 20 MPa√m at −20 °C. A plate carries 150 MPa and has an edge crack (Y=1.12). What crack depth causes fracture?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ac​=π1​(1.12⋅15020​)2=π1​(0.1190)2.
  2. ac​=0.01417/π=4.51×10−3 m, so 4.5 mm.
  3. A crack that size in a weld is easy to miss. That’s how the Liberty ships failed, and why modern steels are specified with toughness at the lowest service temperature.

09.13.title: Fatigue
09.13.html:
Bend a paper clip once and it’s fine. Bend it back and forth twenty times and it snaps, although no single bend was strong enough to break it. Most mechanical failures in service are like this: a bike crank, an axle, a wind turbine bolt, each loaded far below its tensile strength, but millions of times. That’s fatigue. A tiny crack starts at a stress concentration (a scratch, a sharp corner, a weld toe), grows a little with each cycle, and the part breaks suddenly once the crack reaches its critical size (09.12).

The S-N curve

Test many specimens at different fully reversed stress amplitudes σa​ and record the cycles to failure N. On log-log axes the data fall on a straight line, Basquin’s law:

σa​=σf′​(2N)b,

with b typically between −0.05 and −0.12. Steels show an apparent endurance limit near 106 to 107 cycles, often about half the tensile strength for polished specimens. Aluminium has none: it always fails eventually, which is why aircraft structures have a finite certified life.

Mean stress

Most real loads aren’t fully reversed. A bolt is preloaded, then vibrates. A tensile mean stress σm​ opens cracks and shortens life. The Goodman line converts the pair to an equivalent fully reversed amplitude:

σar​σa​​+σu​σm​​=1⇒σar​=1−σm​/σu​σa​​.

Variable loading: Miner’s rule

If a part sees ni​ cycles at amplitude si​, where it would last Ni​ cycles, each block uses up a fraction ni​/Ni​ of its life. It fails when

D=i∑​Ni​ni​​=1.

Miner’s rule is crude (actual failures range from D=0.3 to 3) but it’s the standard design starting point.

Designing against fatigue

Avoid sharp corners, polish surfaces, and put critical welds in low-stress regions. Shot peening adds compressive residual stress at the surface. Keep the stress range low, and remember that a few large cycles can do more damage than many small ones.

Worked exampleFitting and using an S-N curve

Steel with σf′​=1225 MPa, b=−0.095, σu​=725 MPa.

  1. Six synthetic tests from 650 MPa (575 cycles) to 350 MPa (256 000 cycles), with scatter of 0.08 in log₁₀N. A log-log least-squares fit gives σf′​=1232 MPa and b=−0.0959, close to the true values.
  2. Strength at 106 cycles: 1225(2×106)−0.095=308.7 MPa, 0.43 times the UTS.
  3. A shaft with amplitude 250 MPa and mean 150 MPa: Goodman gives 250/(1−150/725)=315.2 MPa. The life is 8.0×105 cycles, against 9.2×106 with zero mean. A modest mean stress cuts the life more than tenfold.
  4. Daily loading of 20 cycles at 450 MPa, 300 at 380 and 3000 at 320: the damage per day is 8.11×10−3, so Miner predicts 123 days. The 3000 small cycles do 54 % of the damage and the 20 big ones 13 %.

Exercise 1A preloaded bolt

A bolt of the same steel has a mean stress of 400 MPa from preload and a vibrating amplitude of 60 MPa. What’s the equivalent fully reversed amplitude, and is the life above 107 cycles?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. σar​=60/(1−400/725)=60/0.4483=133.8 MPa.
  2. N=21​(133.8/1225)1/(−0.095). log10​(133.8/1225)=−0.9617, divided by −0.095 gives 10.121, so N=0.5×1010.121=6.6×109 cycles.
  3. Yes, well above 107. High preload is good for bolts because the bolt then sees only a small share of the external load variation (Phase 06).

09.14.title: Corrosion
09.14.html:
Leave a steel bolt on a beach in Bali and in a few months it’s orange and flaking. Corrosion costs industrial countries around 3 % of GDP a year: rusted bridges, leaking pipes, failed fasteners. It’s electrochemistry. Metal atoms give up electrons and dissolve as ions at an anode; somewhere nearby, a cathode consumes those electrons, usually by reducing oxygen dissolved in water. Salt water makes a good electrolyte to carry the ions, which is why the coast is so harsh.

Faraday’s law

Each dissolved atom of valence n releases n electrons, so a current I flowing for time t removes a mass

m=nFItM​,

with M the molar mass and F=96485 C/mol. Divide by density and area and you get the penetration rate from the corrosion current density i:

x˙=nFρiM​.

For steel, 1 µA/cm² means about 0.012 mm per year.

Galvanic corrosion

Two different metals in electrical contact in an electrolyte form a battery. The more active one (lower in the galvanic series: magnesium, zinc, aluminium, steel, then copper, stainless steel, titanium, gold) becomes the anode and corrodes faster. The cathode is protected.

The current is limited mostly by how much oxygen the cathode can reduce, so a large cathode and small anode is the worst case: the whole current crowds into a little anode. Steel rivets in a copper sheet fail quickly; copper rivets in a steel sheet are fine.

Protection

  • Barriers: paint, galvanising (zinc coating), anodising aluminium.
  • Sacrificial anodes: blocks of zinc or aluminium bolted to a boat hull or buried pipeline. They corrode in place of the steel and are replaced periodically.
  • Impressed current from a power supply, for large structures.
  • Design: avoid crevices and water traps, insulate dissimilar metals, choose stainless steel or aluminium where appropriate.

Worked exampleRates and anode sizing

  1. 1 A for a year dissolves 1⋅3.156×107⋅55.845/(2⋅96485)=9.13 kg of iron.
  2. At 1 µA/cm²: iron thins by 11.6 µm per year, zinc by 15.0, aluminium by 10.9, copper by 11.6.
  3. A 2 mA galvanic current into a 1000 cm² steel anode is 2 µA/cm², 0.023 mm per year. The same current into a 10 cm² anode is 200 µA/cm², 2.32 mm per year: 100 times faster.
  4. A boat hull needs 0.3 A of protection for 2 years. Zinc consumed is 0.3⋅6.31×107⋅65.38/(2⋅96485)=6.42 kg. Allowing 90 % current efficiency and using only 85 % of the anode before replacement, fit 8.4 kg.

Exercise 1An aluminium hull

An aluminium boat hull is protected by sacrificial aluminium-zinc-indium alloy anodes, which have a capacity of about 2500 A h/kg. How many kilograms are needed for 0.2 A over 3 years?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Charge: 0.2⋅3⋅8766=5260 A h.
  2. Mass: 5260/2500=2.1 kg.
  3. Compare zinc: about 780 A h/kg in practice, so 6.7 kg. Aluminium alloy anodes are lighter for the same protection, which is why they’re popular on boats.

09.15.title: Material selection
09.15.html:
Why are bike frames made of steel, aluminium, titanium, carbon fibre and even bamboo, but never concrete? Why are aircraft wing skins aluminium or composite, and roof beams wood or steel? Choosing a material isn’t about finding the “strongest”. It’s about which material does a specific job at the lowest mass or cost. Mike Ashby’s method turns that into a ranking with one number.

Performance indices

Write the quantity to minimise (mass) in terms of the design requirement (stiffness), the fixed geometry (length) and the free variable (cross-section size). Then eliminate the free variable.

A light stiff tie, length L, needing axial stiffness S=EA/L: the area must be A=SL/E, so

m=ρAL=SL2Eρ​.

Maximise E/ρ.

A light stiff beam with a square section of side b, needing bending stiffness ∝EI/L3 with I=b4/12: b2∝(SL3/E)1/2, so

m=ρb2L∝E1/2ρ​.

Maximise E1/2/ρ. Low density counts for more, because a lighter material can be made thicker, and stiffness grows faster than area.

A light stiff panel (fixed width and length, free thickness): maximise E1/3/ρ.

For strength-limited beams the index is σf2/3​/ρ; for cost, replace ρ by ρCm​ (price per kg).

Ashby charts

On log-log axes of E against ρ, each index is a straight line: E/ρ=C has slope 1, E1/2/ρ=C has slope 2, E1/3/ρ=C has slope 3. All materials on one line perform equally. Slide the line up: the materials still above it are the best.

Worked exampleA 1 m cantilever

A 1 m square-section cantilever must deflect no more than 5 mm under 1 kN at the tip. Size it in each material (I=PL3/(3Eδ), b=(12I)1/4) and weigh it:

  1. Spruce 3.67 kg, bamboo 4.67, CFRP (quasi-isotropic, 70 GPa) 5.27, aluminium 9.13, GFRP 10.75, titanium 11.87, concrete 12.39, steel 15.32, ABS 19.58.
  2. The order is exactly the ranking by E1/2/ρ, and mass times index is the same constant for every material to 10−12.
  3. By cost (rough prices per kg): bamboo 4.67 USD, spruce 5.51, steel 12.26, aluminium 22.82, CFRP 211.
  4. Ties (E/ρ) rank differently: CFRP, then steel, spruce and aluminium almost tied. Panels (E1/3/ρ): spruce, bamboo, CFRP, GFRP.
  5. Concrete looks fine for a stiff beam but its tensile strength is only 4 MPa, so it fails the strength check. Real selection always screens several requirements.

Exercise 1Steel against aluminium

For a light stiff beam, how much heavier is steel (E=210 GPa, ρ=7850 kg/m³) than aluminium (E=70 GPa, ρ=2700 kg/m³)? And for a tie?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Beam: mass ratio =(ρs​/ρa​)(Ea​/Es​)1/2=2.907⋅0.5774=1.68.
  2. Tie: (ρs​/ρa​)(Ea​/Es​)=2.907/3=0.969. Steel is slightly lighter as a tie.
  3. Bending favours low density, which is why aluminium wins for frames and panels, while steel cables are fine.

quiz.q: Beam mass ratio steel/aluminium (E^1/2/ρ index). 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: (ρs​/ρa​)Ea​/Es​​.

quiz.q: Panel mass ratio steel/aluminium (E^1/3/ρ index). 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: Low density counts even more for panels.

quiz.q: Slope of the E^1/2/ρ guideline on a log E against log ρ chart.
quiz.explain: log E = 2 log ρ + const.

quiz.q: For a light, stiff tie you maximise…
quiz.explain: Mass ∝ ρ/E.

quiz.q: Why does wood beat steel for a light stiff beam?
quiz.explain: The index E^1/2/ρ rewards low density.
options: Its low density lets the section grow, and I grows fast with size

09.16.title: Embodied energy and carbon
09.16.html:
Every kilogram of material has already cost energy before you use it: mining, refining, smelting, rolling. Making primary aluminium from bauxite takes around 200 MJ/kg, mostly electricity for electrolysis. Recycling it takes about 30. Steel takes about 25, sawn timber under 10. As grids decarbonise and emissions get priced, engineers increasingly have to choose materials for their whole life, not just their performance.

Embodied energy and carbon

The embodied energy Hm​ (MJ/kg) and embodied carbon cm​ (kg CO₂ per kg) of a material are the totals from cradle to factory gate. Typical rough values:

Material MJ/kg kg CO₂/kg
Steel 25 2.0
Primary aluminium 200 12
Recycled aluminium 30 2
Titanium 600 40
CFRP 270 25
Bamboo 3 0.4
Spruce 8 0.5
Concrete 1.1 0.13

They vary with the source and the electricity mix, so treat them as factors of two, not three significant figures.

Selecting for low energy

Replace density by ρHm​ in the performance index (09.15). For a light stiff beam, minimum energy means maximising

ρHm​E1/2​.

The use phase

For anything that moves, mass costs energy throughout its life. A car consumes roughly 0.35 L of fuel per 100 km for every extra 100 kg. Over 200 000 km that’s about 240 MJ for every kilogram it carries. Lightweighting pays back when the fuel saved exceeds the extra production energy:

Δm⋅Euse​>mnew​Hnew​−mold​Hold​.

A full life-cycle assessment adds manufacturing, transport and end of life (recycling credit or landfill).

Worked exampleThe cantilever and a car panel

  1. Cantilever (09.15) energies: steel 15.32 kg and 383 MJ; primary aluminium 9.13 kg but 1826 MJ; recycled aluminium 274 MJ; titanium 7121 MJ; CFRP 1424 MJ; bamboo 14 MJ; spruce 29 MJ.
  2. Carbon: steel 30.6 kg CO₂, primary aluminium 110, CFRP 132, spruce 1.8, bamboo 1.9.
  3. Energy is exactly proportional to ρHm​/E1/2 across all the materials, as the index predicts.
  4. Car panel: 10 kg of steel replaced by aluminium sized for equal panel stiffness, 10/2.016=4.96 kg. Production goes from 250 to 992 MJ (742 MJ more). Fuel saved over 200 000 km: 5.04⋅239=1206 MJ, a net gain of 464 MJ. Payback after 123 000 km.
  5. With recycled aluminium, production drops to 149 MJ, 101 MJ less than steel, so the lighter panel is ahead from the first kilometre.

Exercise 1A carbon bike frame

A steel bike frame weighs 2.2 kg; a carbon one 1.0 kg. Using the table, what is the embodied energy of each? A rider has a mass of 75 kg; does the lighter frame save meaningful energy over its life?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Steel: 2.2⋅25=55 MJ. Carbon: 1.0⋅270=270 MJ.
  2. The carbon frame costs 215 MJ more to make, about the energy in 6 litres of petrol.
  3. A bicycle is human powered and 1.2 kg is about 1.5 % of rider plus bike, so the energy saving over its life is tiny. The choice is about performance and feel, not energy. For a car or aircraft the picture is reversed.

quiz.q: Embodied energy (MJ) of 4.96 kg of primary aluminium at 200 MJ/kg.
quiz.explain: mHm​.

quiz.q: Fuel energy (MJ) to carry 1 kg for 200 000 km at 0.35 L/100 km per 100 kg, 34.2 MJ/L. 1 decimal.
Extra embodied energy (MJ) of the carbon bike frame over the steel one.
For a minimum-energy stiff beam you maximise…
quiz.explain: Replace ρ by ρH_m.

quiz.q: Why is recycled aluminium so much better than primary?
quiz.explain: About 85 % less energy.
options: Remelting needs far less energy than electrolysis of alumina

09.17.title: Choosing a process
09.17.html:
You’ve designed an aluminium bracket. Should it be machined from a block, sand cast, die cast or 3D printed? Each process makes it with different tolerances and finishes, but usually the decision comes down to how many you need. A die-casting mould might cost 40 000 USD and then turn out a part every 30 seconds for pennies; a CNC machine needs almost no tooling but takes 15 minutes per part.

Screening

First rule out processes that can’t make the part at all:

  • Material: you can’t die cast steel or injection mould titanium.
  • Shape: hollow, thin-walled, undercuts, overhangs.
  • Size and mass: from grams (die casting, moulding) to tonnes (sand casting).
  • Tolerance and roughness: machining reaches ±0.01 mm and Ra 0.8 µm; sand casting about ±1 mm and Ra 12 µm.

Cost model

Among the survivors, Ashby’s cost model splits the unit cost into three parts:

C=1−fmCm​​+nCt​​+n˙C˙L​​,
  • material: part mass m, price Cm​ per kg, scrap fraction f;
  • tooling Ct​ (moulds, dies, fixtures) shared over a batch of n;
  • overhead rate C˙L​ (machine, labour, energy per hour) divided by the production rate n˙.

At small batches tooling dominates; at large batches the cost falls to a floor of material plus time. Two processes cost the same when

n∗=(floor)a​−(floor)b​Ct,b​−Ct,a​​.

Rough guide: 3D print 1 to 10, machine 10 to a few hundred, sand cast hundreds to thousands, die cast or mould above 10 000.

Worked exampleA 250 g aluminium bracket

Aluminium at 3 USD/kg. Processes (scrap fraction, tooling, rate per hour, parts per hour): CNC (0.60, 300, 80, 4); sand casting (0.30, 2000, 50, 10); die casting (0.10, 40 000, 120, 120); metal 3D print (0.05, 0, 60, 0.5).

  1. One part: printing 120.79 USD, CNC 321.88, sand 2006, die casting 40 002.
  2. 100 parts: CNC 24.88, sand 26.07, die casting 401.83, printing 120.79.
  3. 10 000 parts: die casting 5.83, sand 6.27, CNC 21.91.
  4. Crossovers: CNC beats printing above 3 parts, sand casting beats CNC above 108, die casting beats sand casting above 8966. At each crossover the two unit costs agree to 10−9.
  5. Printing never wins beyond a couple of parts here. It wins when the shape is impossible otherwise, such as internal channels or lattices.

Exercise 1Injection moulding a plastic part

An ABS housing can be printed (0 tooling, 6 USD per part in material and time) or injection moulded (mould 15 000 USD, 0.40 USD per part). Above what batch size is moulding cheaper?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Equal cost: 6=15000/n+0.40.
  2. n=15000/5.60=2679.
  3. Above about 2700 parts, mould. Many products start with printed or machined prototypes and switch once the design is frozen and volume justifies the tool.

Unit cost (USD) of the die-cast bracket at n = 1000. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Material 0.83 + tooling 40 + time 1.

quiz.q: Material cost (USD) of the CNC bracket including scrap (60 % scrap, 0.25 kg, 3 USD/kg). 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: mCm​/(1−f).

quiz.q: At very large batch sizes, unit cost approaches…
quiz.explain: Tooling per part → 0.
options: Material plus machine time per part

quiz.q: Which process best suits 5 complex titanium brackets with internal cooling channels?
quiz.explain: No tooling; internal features are free.

09.18.title: Metal cutting
09.18.html:
Watch a lathe turning steel and a hot blue ribbon curls off the tool. That chip isn’t torn off: the metal ahead of the tool is sheared intensely in a narrow zone, the shear plane, then slides up the tool’s face. Nearly all the power goes into that shearing and into friction, and ends up as heat. Merchant’s 1945 model of this zone still gives good estimates of cutting forces, which you need to size machine tools, fixtures and workholding.

Orthogonal cutting

Model the tool as a straight edge perpendicular to the motion, removing a layer of thickness t0​ (the feed) and width w (the depth of cut).

  • The rake angle α is the tilt of the tool face from vertical. Positive rake is a sharper tool.
  • The shear angle ϕ is the angle of the shear plane from the cutting direction.
  • Friction on the rake face, coefficient μ=tanβ.

The chip comes off thicker than the cut. Volume conservation gives the chip ratio

r=tc​t0​​=cos(ϕ−α)sinϕ​.

Forces

The force to shear the material is Fs​=τs​t0​w/sinϕ, with τs​ the shear flow stress. Resolving the resultant (which lies at angle β−α from the cutting direction):

Fc​=sinϕcos(ϕ+β−α)τs​t0​wcos(β−α)​,Ft​=Fc​tan(β−α).

Merchant assumed the shear plane sits where Fc​ is smallest. Setting dFc​/dϕ=0:

ϕ=45∘+2α​−2β​.

The cutting power is P=Fc​V, so the specific cutting energy u=Fc​/(t0​w) (in J/mm³ or N/mm²) multiplied by the removal rate gives the spindle power.

Worked exampleTurning medium-carbon steel

Rake 10°, μ=0.5 (β=26.57°), τs​=550 MPa, feed 0.2 mm, depth 2 mm, 200 m/min.

  1. ϕ=45+5−13.28=36.717°. Brute-force minimisation of Fc​ over ϕ gives 36.718°, within the 0.0001° grid.
  2. Chip ratio sin36.72°/cos26.72°=0.669: the chip is 0.299 mm thick.
  3. Fc​=590 N, Ft​=175 N. Power 590⋅3.33=1.97 kW.
  4. Specific cutting energy 1475 N/mm². Handbooks give 1.5 to 2.5 J/mm³ for this steel; real tools add edge rounding and ploughing.
  5. Rake 0°: Fc​=712 N. Rake 20°: 494 N. More rake cuts more easily but weakens the edge, so carbide tools for steel run near 0 to 10°.

Exercise 1Removal rate and power

A 5 kW lathe cuts the same steel with u=2.0 J/mm³ (a realistic value). At depth 3 mm and feed 0.25 mm, what is the highest cutting speed (m/min) the motor allows at 80 % efficiency?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Available cutting power: 0.8⋅5=4 kW.
  2. Removal rate: 4000/2.0=2000 mm³/s.
  3. V=2000/(3⋅0.25)=2667 mm/s, which is 160 m/min.

quiz.q: Merchant shear angle (degrees) for α = 0° and μ = 0.8. 2 decimals.
Chip ratio for φ = 30° and α = 10°. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: sinϕ/cos(ϕ−α).

quiz.q: Highest cutting speed (m/min) in the exercise.
quiz.explain: Power / (u × area).

quiz.q: Increasing friction on the rake face…
options: Lowers the shear angle and raises the cutting force

quiz.q: Where does most of the cutting power end up?
quiz.explain: Shear and friction are dissipative.
options: As heat in the chip, tool and workpiece
